cues.say: Every pet here is a real pothole complaint filed with NYC 311 in Queens Community Board 13 — 2,512 of them.
Their fates follow the city record: adopted when DOT repairs them, ghosts when nobody finds them, feral when they wait more than 60 days.
Feral of the week is picked by the calendar, not by merit. This one has been waiting since the date on its record.
Filter by outcome and age. Hundreds of complaints have been open for over a year: that is the real backlog.
A pet page: name, temperament and a bio. The bio may only restate facts from the record; Gemini restyles it and a fact guard rejects any changed date, number or street.
Location is rounded to about 100 metres. No house numbers, ever.
The status timeline: every change cites the complaint field that caused it. The sync is the only thing that can change an outcome.
The complaint history is the city's record, exactly as published.
And here is that complaint on NYC Open Data. Nothing is invented.
Only 38 percent of complaints have coordinates, so the map holds fewer than half the shelter.
The rest are lost strays: complaints about a stretch of street between two cross streets. We list them by street instead of guessing a point.
The ghost hall: the city inspected and didn't find the reported problem. Not anyone's fault — potholes get patched, or move on.
Anyone can leave a pet an adoption note. It is filtered, rate-limited, and stored privately.
It starts an adoption-moderation workflow and waits. Nothing a visitor types is public until a person approves it in the Shelter Office.
The sync log: last sync time, every run, and the unmapped phrases we refuse to guess.
The public mirror of the Shelter Office, with live workflow state: a lifecycle instance for every open pet, and the review queues.
